text: A private equity firm is about to buy a chain of after-school tutoring centers, and management says revenue will double in five years. You lead the commercial due diligence: is the plan believable, and what should the buyer actually count on?
EY-Parthenon cases are usually candidate-led: you build the structure, decide what to dig into, and ask for data. Many first-round cases are commercial due diligence for private equity buyers.

Put simply, they want structured thinking, real comfort with numbers like growth rates and multiples, and a clear point of view. Interviewers push back on "it depends" answers. Formats vary by office, so confirm the details with your recruiter.

Usually an online numbers test first, sometimes with a recorded video interview. First round: one or two interviews of 45 to 60 minutes, each mixing fit questions with a candidate-led case. Final round: two or three interviews with senior leaders. Some offices add a group case or a written case you present in a few slides.

A structure built for the question, not a memorized template. Quant fluency: growth rates, margins, payback, and multiples. A hypothesis you test with data, not a list of ideas. A decisive answer: what number would you underwrite?

Market. Is demand growing, and why? Competition. Who else is fighting for these customers, and on what terms? Customers. Why do they buy, would they pay more, and will they stay? The plan. Does management's forecast hold up, lever by lever? The answer. The number the buyer should actually count on.
MarketGrowing, and why? CompetitionWho's winning? CustomersWhy they buy and stay. The planDoes it hold up?
Commercial due diligenceA deep check of a company's market, competitors, and customers before a buyer commits. It answers one question: will the business plan come true?
Management caseThe forecast the company's own leaders put together. It's usually optimistic, because it helps the sale price.
Diligence caseThe more cautious forecast the consultants build after testing every assumption. The buyer prices the deal on this one.
UnderwriteTo commit to a number. "We'd underwrite 140 million" means "that's the revenue we'd base our price on."
CAGRCompound annual growth rate: the steady yearly growth that gets you from start to finish. Doubling in five years is about 15 percent a year.
Rule of 7272 divided by the growth rate gives the years to double. At 8 percent a year, revenue doubles in about 9 years.
LeverOne driver of the forecast, like number of centers, students per center, or price. Testing levers one at a time keeps the math clean.
ChurnThe share of customers who leave each period. Higher churn means a center has to enroll more students just to stay flat.
Price sensitivityHow much demand drops when price rises. Surveys often ask, "What would you do if the price went up 10 percent?"
Voice of the customerSurveys and interviews with customers. In due diligence, it's often the most convincing evidence.

Our client is Calder Peak Partners, a private equity firm. It's in exclusive talks to buy Brightwell Tutoring, a chain of 150 after-school math and reading centers for kids in grades 1 through 12, across the Southeast and Texas.

Brightwell makes about 90 million dollars in revenue. Management's plan says revenue will double to 180 million in five years, by opening more centers, raising prices, and enrolling more students per center.
Calder Peak has asked us for a commercial due diligence: is management's plan realistic, and what revenue should Calder Peak count on in year five?
Restate the question in one sentence, then say what you'd like to clarify.

"So Calder Peak wants to know whether Brightwell can really double revenue to 180 million in five years, and if not, what year-five revenue it should count on instead. Is that right? I have a few quick questions before I structure it."
Interviewer: "Sure, go ahead." In a candidate-led case, the wheel is yours from this point on.
Ask two or three clarifying questions. Pick ones whose answers would change your approach.
How does management plan to double revenue?Three levers: open 15 new centers a year, raise prices about 4 percent a year, and grow students per center from 100 to 110.
How fast has Brightwell grown recently?About 10 new centers a year for the last four years, and revenue growth of about 8 percent a year.
What do families pay?About 500 dollars a month on average, for two sessions a week. That's about 6,000 dollars a year per student.
Who are the competitors?Other tutoring chains, local independent tutors, and fast-growing online and AI tutoring apps that cost much less.
What does the deal team need from us?A diligence-case revenue forecast for year five that they can put in their model, in three weeks.
The first two questions are the most valuable: they turn the plan into levers, and they give you a track record to compare it with.
Okay. How do you want to approach this?
Take 60 seconds to sketch your structure. Then walk through it, say where you'd start, and ask for specific data.

"This is a commercial due diligence, so I'd look at the market, the competition, and the customers, then test management's plan lever by lever. First, the market: how many families in Brightwell's states pay for tutoring, and is that growing? Second, competition, especially cheaper online and AI tutoring. Third, customers: why parents choose Brightwell, how long they stay, and how they'd react to price increases. Fourth, the plan itself: new centers, students per center, and price. The plan needs about 15 percent growth a year, when Brightwell has been growing about 8, so my hypothesis is that it's too aggressive. I'd like to start with market and company trends."

It mirrors how real due diligence is organized: market, competition, customers, then the plan. It turns a big forecast into three levers you can test one at a time. It compares the plan's growth with the track record right away, which gives you a sharp hypothesis.
If you blank, "market, competition, customers, plan" works for almost any due diligence case.
Here's what you asked for: six years of market and company data. What stands out?
Which finding should you lead with?
The number of students is growing fast, so the plan looks easy.
Demand is leveling off and moving online, where prices are falling fast. Brightwell's students per center are flat and more families are leaving, so growing to 110 students per center will be hard.
Online tutoring is shrinking.
Brightwell's churn is falling, so students per center will rise.

The number of kids barely moved. The share of families paying for tutoring went from 14 to 19 percent, but it has stopped rising. Meanwhile, online's share of spending more than doubled, from 18 to 42 percent, and online prices fell by half. At Brightwell, students per center have been flat at about 100 for four years, and monthly churn rose from 2.5 to 3.3 percent. The plan's jump to 110 students per center goes against every trend here.
Say the insight, tie it to the plan, and ask for your next piece of data.

"The market is maturing and moving online. The share of families paying for tutoring has stopped rising, online's share of spending more than doubled, and online prices halved. At Brightwell, students per center have been flat at 100 for four years while churn keeps rising. So the plan's jump to 110 students looks unlikely, and price increases could push more families online. Do we have any customer data on price sensitivity and why families leave?"
Notice the pattern: insight, then so-what for the plan, then your own next ask. That's how you move a candidate-led case forward.
Good instinct. We surveyed 1,000 current Brightwell parents. Here's how they say they'd react to price increases. What's your read?
What's the so-what?
Parents don't care about price.
Small price increases are safe, but bigger ones push many families away. So price is a smaller lever than the plan assumes.
Brightwell should raise prices 15 percent right away.
In-person tutoring has no advantage over online.

At 3 to 5 percent, only 2 to 4 percent of parents say they'd leave, so revenue still rises a little. At 10 percent, 15 percent would leave, and revenue falls. Price increases also stack up: 4 percent a year for five years adds up to about 22 percent, and families feel the total, not each step. The good news is that parents value in-person tutors who know their child, which supports a modest, steady premium.
Synthesize both exhibits in three sentences, and say how you'd rebuild the forecast.

"The market is flattening and shifting online, students per center are flat, and churn is rising, so the plan's growth in students per center looks unlikely. On price, about 3 percent a year is safe, but larger increases push families toward cheaper online options. So I'd rebuild the forecast with flat students per center, 3 percent price increases, and Brightwell's actual pace of about 10 new centers a year."
This is the heart of commercial due diligence: take the plan apart lever by lever, replace each assumption with one the evidence supports, and put it back together.
Walk me through management's 180 million, then rebuild it the way you'd underwrite it.
Say the formula first: revenue equals centers times students per center times price. Rebuild management's number, then swap in the evidence, one lever at a time.

Step 1. Management's plan. 150 centers plus 15 a year for five years is 225 centers. Each center has 110 students paying about 7,300 dollars a year, or about 800 thousand dollars. 225 times 800 thousand is 180 million.
Step 2. Centers. At Brightwell's actual pace of 10 a year, it reaches 200 centers, not 225.
Step 3. Price. 3 percent a year adds up to about 16 percent over five years. 6,000 dollars times 1.16 is about 7,000 dollars a year.
Step 4. Revenue per center. Students stay flat at 100. 100 times 7,000 dollars is 700 thousand dollars per center.
Step 5. Diligence case. 200 centers times 700 thousand is 140 million dollars. That's 40 million, or about 22 percent, below management's plan.

Step 6. Growth check. 90 million to 140 million is about 55 percent over five years, roughly 9 percent a year, close to the 8 percent track record. The plan needs about 15 percent a year, since doubling in five years is 72 divided by 5.
Quick check: what's revenue per center in the diligence case?
600 thousand dollars
700 thousand dollars
800 thousand dollars
7 million dollars
100 students times 7,000 dollars a year is 700 thousand. Everyday version: a center with 100 kids, each paying about 580 dollars a month, brings in about 700 thousand a year.
Summarize the math in two sentences, and add one sanity check.

"Management's plan needs about 15 percent growth a year, nearly double Brightwell's track record. Rebuilt with 10 new centers a year, flat students per center, and 3 percent price increases, year-five revenue comes to about 140 million, 40 million below plan. That's about 9 percent a year, which is close to what Brightwell has actually delivered, so it passes the sanity check."

If the interviewer asks, "Isn't that too conservative?": "It assumes nothing gets worse. If online keeps taking share, students per center could fall. I'd show 140 million as the base case, an upside of about 155 million if Brightwell opens 12 centers a year and reaches 105 students per center, and a downside if churn keeps rising."
Here are the risks the team flagged. Score each for likelihood and impact, from 1 to 5, with one reason for each. Which three should the deal team dig into before bidding?
Score each risk out loud with a one-line reason, then name your top three.

"I'd dig into three. First, online and AI tutoring, because it threatens both students per center and price. Second, new-center performance: the plan needs 15 openings a year when the track record is 10. Third, price sensitivity, since the survey shows a cliff above 5 percent. Hiring tutors matters, but it's more a cost issue than a revenue one."
Which three come first?
R1, R2, and R3: online and AI tutoring, new-center performance, and price sensitivity.
R4, R5, and R6: tutor hiring, a recession, and a manager leaving.
R1, R5, and R6.
All six at once, with equal effort.

R1, R2, and R3 each hit one of the plan's three levers directly, and the exhibits already show warning signs. R4 is real but mostly affects costs. R5 could hurt, but tutoring tends to hold up because parents protect spending on their kids. R6 is small for a chain of 150 centers.
The deal partner just walked in. You have 60 seconds. What should Calder Peak count on?
Lead with the number. Then three reasons, the main risk, and next steps.
"Calder Peak should underwrite about 140 million of year-five revenue, not management's 180 million, and price the deal on that."
"First, the market is maturing. The share of families paying for tutoring has stopped rising, and spending is moving online, where prices have halved."
"Second, Brightwell's own numbers don't support the jump. Students per center have been flat at about 100 for four years, churn is rising, and it has opened about 10 centers a year, not 15."
"Third, price is a smaller lever than management thinks. The survey says about 3 percent a year is safe, but bigger increases push families to cheaper online options."

"It's still an attractive business: parents value tutors who know their child, and 9 percent growth a year is solid. The main risk is online and AI tutoring, which could push the number lower. Next steps: survey families who left, test a hybrid plan that mixes in-person and online sessions, and visit five of the newest centers to see how fast they fill up."
Week 1CustomersSurvey 300 families who left.Try the top online rivals as a customer would.
Week 2CentersCompare the last 40 openings by the year they opened.Visit five of the newest centers.
Week 3ForecastBuild base, upside, and downside cases.Hand the model to the deal team.

Students per center. Target: at least 100. Families leaving each month. Target: back below 3 percent. New centers opened. Target: 10 to 12 a year. Yearly price increase. Target: about 3 percent, with no jump in churn.
Estimate how much U.S. families spend on K-12 tutoring in a year.
Go top-down. Start with students, narrow to those who get paid tutoring, then multiply by yearly spend. Say each assumption out loud.
Start broad. There are about 55 million K-12 students in the U.S.
Times about 15 percent who get paid tutoring in a year. That's about 8 million students.
Times about 2,000 dollars a year each. Most kids get far less than Brightwell's full program. That's about 16 billion dollars.
Split it. If about 60 percent is in-person, that's about 10 billion dollars in-person and 6 billion online.
Sanity check. Brightwell's 90 million is under 1 percent of the in-person market, so this is a market of many small players, which is typical for a private equity roll-up.

Growth check. If the market grows 4 percent a year, it doubles in about 18 years. Brightwell growing 9 percent means it's taking share. The interviewer is grading your structure, not the exact number.
As AI tutors get better and cheaper, will in-person tutoring keep growing?
Split growth into more students and more spend per student, then list drivers and headwinds.
AccountabilityParents pay for a person who shows up, tracks progress, and keeps their kid on task.
Learning gapsMany students are behind in math and reading, and parents want help catching up.
Childcare valueAfter-school sessions also give working parents a safe place for their kids.
Hybrid modelsCenters that add online practice between sessions can charge more and keep families longer.
AI tutors are cheap, always available, and improving fast. Online prices keep falling, which puts a ceiling on in-person prices. Tutor wages are rising, which squeezes margins.

Say the market is 100 today, with 58 spent in-person. If the whole market grows to 120 but in-person's share drops to 40 percent, in-person spending is 48, down from 58. A growing market can still mean a shrinking slice.

"In-person will shrink as a share, but it won't disappear, because parents pay for accountability and a person who knows their child. The winners will blend in-person sessions with online practice, so I'd make a hybrid offer part of Calder Peak's plan."
